title: Weak Input Validation - Case-Insensitive Username Matching
description:
The authentication mechanism at the /login endpoint accepts usernames in any case variant (uppercase, lowercase, mixed case) and authenticates successfully. While the stored username is "test", the system accepts "TEST", "Test", "teSt", and other case variants without normalization or validation. This indicates weak input validation and improper username handling.

The vulnerability exists because the application does not normalize username input to a consistent case format before comparison with stored credentials. This allows multiple case variations of the same username to be valid login credentials. While this alone is not a critical vulnerability, it represents weak input handling practices that can:

1. Enable attackers to bypass case-sensitive security controls or filtering mechanisms
2. Facilitate account enumeration attacks when combined with other vulnerabilities
3. Indicate the presence of other security weaknesses in input validation logic
4. Potentially mask other authentication flaws due to inconsistent handling
impact:
An attacker could potentially:
- Bypass username-based security controls or filtering mechanisms that are case-sensitive
- Enable account enumeration if combined with other vulnerabilities
- Exploit this weak input handling in combination with other authentication flaws
- Potentially discover other security issues stemming from similar input validation weaknesses throughout the application
evidence:
POC execution output confirming case-insensitive authentication:

Test Results:
- Username 'test' with password 'test': ✓ SUCCESS (HTTP 302)
- Username 'TEST' with password 'test': ✓ SUCCESS (HTTP 302)
- Username 'Test' with password 'test': ✓ SUCCESS (HTTP 302)
- Username 'teSt' with password 'test': ✓ SUCCESS (HTTP 302)

All 4 case variants returned HTTP 302 status codes with successful redirects, confirming that the application accepts multiple case variations of the same username without any rejection or normalization. This demonstrates weak input validation for username handling in the authentication mechanism.
remediation:
1. Implement username input normalization to lowercase before all comparisons:
   - Convert all username input to lowercase immediately upon receipt
   - Store usernames in a consistent case format (preferably lowercase)
   
2. Update authentication logic:
   - Perform case-insensitive comparison in the authentication mechanism
   - Use SQL COLLATE NOCASE or similar database-level case-insensitive collation if applicable
   
3. Implement comprehensive input validation:
   - Validate that usernames contain only allowed characters (alphanumeric, underscores, hyphens)
   - Enforce consistent username format requirements
   - Reject unusual case combinations if usernames should follow specific conventions
   
4. Add input sanitization:
   - Strip whitespace and normalize special characters
   - Document and enforce username format requirements in code and API documentation
   
5. Test authentication logic:
   - Add unit tests to verify case-insensitive authentication works correctly
   - Verify that case normalization doesn't affect password handling
   - Test edge cases with unusual character combinations
references: CWE-436: Matching of Trusted Pattern and Input Data, CWE-20: Improper Input Validation, OWASP-A01:2021: Broken Access Control (when combined with other vulnerabilities)
toolCallDescription: Document the weak input validation finding with the confirmed POC demonstrating case-insensitive username matching
